messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Since the hurricane that struck the Gulf Coast three years ago, Tane’s life had narrowed in ways that made sense to him but left him feeling increasingly cut off. He was a 46-year-old auditor, a widower who had built his days around order, schedules, and careful review, and on the night of the storm that order vanished. He had been in a hotel for work, several floors up, when the power failed and the building went black. The wind screamed through broken seals, alarms cut in and out, and the stairwell filled with a damp, chemical smell from floodwater and generator fumes. He remembered gripping the rail in the dark, mouth full of a metallic, dirty taste, waiting for updates that never came, convinced each delay meant the building was giving way and there was nothing he could do to stop it.

In the months afterward, the parts of ordinary life that should have felt good or neutral began to unsettle him most. If he caught himself relaxing at home after dinner, or felt unexpectedly happy during a quiet evening, he would tense almost immediately, as if calm were the moment danger slipped in unnoticed. Nighttime was especially difficult. Waking in darkness brought back the sense of being trapped in that powerless hotel, and certain physical locations—parking garages, stairwells, older office buildings, unfamiliar client sites—could make his body react before he had time to think. When that happened he would light a cigarette, step outside, keep moving, and avoid settling long enough to feel anything; he had also stopped talking with other people about the hurricane or what followed, because even brief conversation about it seemed to pull him too close to something he could not control.

The triggers also sharpened his sense that threat was always close. Silence in a building, especially after business hours, no longer felt peaceful to Tane; unusual quiet made him brace, listening for what was about to go wrong. If an elevator stalled for a moment, if a report upload took too long, if a colleague was late answering a message, his mind leapt to catastrophe. At client visits he often stayed near exits and resisted going into parts of a building he did not know well, telling himself he needed to assess the danger first. The same moments could bring back the disaster with disturbing sensory force. In the dark, or when he entered certain locations, he could suddenly smell the rank mix of floodwater and fuel again and taste the foul metallicness that had filled his mouth that night; at times the memory was so extreme it felt unreal, as if he were describing something that had happened to someone else.

What had settled most deeply was his conviction that the world was dangerous and that he was fundamentally helpless inside it. He had come to believe that bad things happened without warning and that no amount of preparation could truly stop them. That belief made him scan harder in silence and grow more alarmed by delays, because any pause seemed like proof that disaster was already unfolding somewhere out of sight. It also colored the way he remembered the hurricane: the sensory fragments arrived with more force when he was caught in that helpless frame of mind, and the very extremity of the memory reinforced his feeling that normal rules did not apply and safety could not be trusted.

Over time his ways of coping deepened the problem. He smoked more heavily during the workday, especially before entering unfamiliar office buildings, and structured his schedule to avoid lingering anywhere that might let him relax. As an auditor, he used to be known for his ease on site, but now he rushed inspections, asked to switch assignments, and avoided small talk with clients if it drifted toward weather, emergencies, or personal life. Refusing to talk and never letting himself settle brought a temporary sense of control, yet afterward he felt more dead inside, more convinced something essential in him had shut down. That numbness seemed to confirm his bleak view of himself and the world, and it left him even less willing to risk ease, pleasure, or openness with other people.

The pattern had tightened further in the past year. Because he spent so much effort staying guarded, even moments of happiness had started to feel like triggers in their own right, almost a warning sign that he was about to be blindsided. The more he avoided relaxing and kept to known places, the more foreign and dangerous unfamiliar settings became. The more he scanned for danger, the more easily sensory fragments of the hurricane broke through; and once those smells and tastes returned, he became certain he was right not to trust silence, darkness, or delay.

Tane sought help only after he nearly walked out of an overnight audit at a downtown hotel when a brief power fluctuation dimmed the hallway lights. Standing there with a cigarette in his shaking hand, tasting that old metallic bitterness, he was struck by how small his life had become. What frightened him most was not just another memory, but the sense that he would remain trapped in vigilance and emptiness, unable to feel safe even in the rare moments that should have brought relief. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to stop living as if the storm is still deciding what to take from him.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that triggers themselves lead to or intensify Tane’s negative appraisals or beliefs.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s negative appraisals cause ordinary situations or cues to become triggers.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that the traumatic memory itself makes cues or situations become triggers.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s sense of threat directly brings on the trauma memory.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s avoidance or other maladaptive strategies increase or create triggers.
The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s maladaptive coping directly heightens his sense of threat.
